name: problem-paragraph
text: Although federated learning keeps patient records within each institution, the gradients and model updates exchanged during training may still expose sensitive information through membership inference or reconstruction attacks. Applying CKKS encryption protects update values, but it increases the serialized communication payload and prevents many poisoning defenses from examining individual plaintext updates. Existing systems may also depend on centralized decryption, unverifiable aggregation, or limited audit evidence, which concentrates trust and reduces accountability. Current approaches therefore seldom provide record-level privacy, practical encrypted communication, poisoning resilience, and independently verifiable governance within one evaluated multi-institutional healthcare framework.

text: Federated learning keeps source records local, but exchanged updates can still leak information. CKKS improves confidentiality while increasing communication cost and hiding the update geometry used by many poisoning defenses. Centralized decryption, unverified aggregation, and limited audit evidence create additional trust concerns. The thesis therefore treats privacy, efficiency, adversarial resilience, and release governance as one engineering problem.

text: This slide shows how the framework transports, aggregates, validates, and releases a model. Mutual TLS and signed round metadata authenticate every submission. The permissioned ledger stores hashes and status, while model ciphertexts remain off-chain. The coordinator performs reputation-weighted homomorphic aggregation and custodians decrypt only the aggregate. Validation either accepts the candidate model or triggers rollback and quarantine. text: This slide explains our main algorithmic contribution, CAABC-FL. Each hospital first adds the previous compression residual to its patient-level differentially private update. The method divides that effective update into contiguous 256-coordinate blocks and scores block energy only after privatization. Every fifth round, the hospitals derive one common support from aggregate block scores, subject to a two-ciphertext packing budget. Each hospital projects onto the same support and retains omitted information as the next residual. The selected blocks occupy aligned CKKS slots, so the coordinator can add ciphertexts without learning client-specific sparse indices. This shared support is the central novelty because it converts logical sparsity into measured encrypted-wire reduction. Formal privacy still comes from the differential privacy accountant, not from compression.

text: The formulation has four parts. First, the global objective is the sample-weighted average of hospital losses, where n_k is the number of records at hospital k and N is the total across participating hospitals. Second, each gradient is clipped to norm C, Gaussian noise z_k^t provides record-level differential privacy, and the residual e_k^t preserves information lost by CAABC-FL compression Q_s_t. Third, the accepted client set A_t contributes encrypted updates to the CKKS sum c_t. Threshold custodians decrypt only this aggregate, and eta_t is the global learning rate. Finally, the design must reduce predictive loss and serialized communication while satisfying privacy, integrity, threshold-release, and audit requirements.

name: single-paragraph-conclusion
text: This thesis developed CAABC-FL as an integrated framework for secure multi-institutional federated learning. The system combines record-level differential privacy, ciphertext-aligned adaptive compression, CKKS-protected aggregation, controlled model release, poisoning-aware validation, and auditable governance within a single workflow. Across the registered experiments, CAABC-FL maintained comparable predictive utility, reduced serialized encrypted upload, limited membership-inference and gradient-reconstruction exposure, and improved resilience under the evaluated poisoning scenarios. These findings demonstrate that privacy, communication efficiency, robustness, and accountability can be addressed together, while broader clinical validation, real multi-host deployment, and dropout-tolerant threshold custody remain necessary before production use.

The experiments support comparable predictive utility, lower serialized encrypted upload, limited exposure under the evaluated privacy attacks, and stronger resilience under the tested poisoning scenarios.
